bridge: You can follow conditions and loops from P02. We will connect the new notation with small rules about fictional accounts.
teaching:
### Turn a sentence into a condition

Suppose a note is readable only when the requester is signed in and owns it. Let A mean “signed in” and B mean “owns the note”. The rule is \(A\land B\), read “A and B”. Both must be true.

OR accepts at least one allowed condition. NOT reverses a condition. A truth table lists possible true/false inputs so you can check the whole rule, not just a favourite example.

### Group things and connect them

A set is a collection of distinct members, such as the allowed note identifiers. Membership asks whether an item belongs to it. A function maps an input to an output under a rule.

A graph has nodes and edges. Nodes can represent computers and edges their allowed connections. A directed edge has a direction; a path follows a sequence of edges.

### Describe change with states

A state machine names the situations a system can be in and which events can move it between them. For an account, ACTIVE and LOCKED might be states. A transition rule says whether a particular event is allowed to change one into the other.

### Support a claim with a reason

A proof explains why a statement follows under its assumptions. One successful example cannot prove a universal claim. One valid counterexample can disprove it. To challenge “every signed-in user may read every note”, show a signed-in user requesting a note owned by someone else.

A guard is the condition that must be true for a transition to happen, such as admin=true for entering maintenance. An invariant is a property that must hold in every reachable allowed state. A rule controlling one transition and a property of every state are related but different claims.
example:
P Q | P AND Q | P implies Q
F F | F       | T
F T | F       | T
T F | F       | F
T T | T       | T

Door states: Locked, Unlocked
unlock: Locked -> Unlocked, requires valid_key
lock: Unlocked -> Locked
Guard (action rule): unlock succeeds only if valid_key is true.
explanation: In the truth table, the implication is false only in row T,F: the stated condition holds but the promised result does not. The door example’s guard is a rule about when an unlock action is allowed. It does not require a key to remain present for as long as a door stays unlocked. Keep that action rule separate from a claim about every persistent state. The balance argument in the teaching section is a complete state-invariant example: start at zero and inspect each permitted balance-changing action.
exercise: Build the truth table for NOT(P AND Q) and compare it with (NOT P) OR (NOT Q). Then add a maintenance transition to the door that requires admin=true. State the guards for the two routes; explain why these are action rules rather than a state invariant.
solution: The two expressions match in all four rows: T,T,T,F for FF,FT,TF,TT. The revised condition is that unlock requires valid_key OR admin, with each transition enforcing its own guard. The normal unlock action requires valid_key; the maintenance action requires admin. These guards control transitions. A state invariant instead describes every reachable state, as the bounded stock property in the challenge does.
challenge: A stock counter starts at 0 and must remain between 0 and 3 inclusive. A receive action adds an integer amount only when 0 <= amount <= 3-stock. A take action subtracts an integer amount only when 0 <= amount <= stock. Without copying the balance proof, explain why both bounds remain true after every action. Then remove the receive upper-bound check and give a sequence that breaks the invariant.
challenge_solution: Base: stock=0 is within [0,3]. Receive adds a non-negative amount, so stock cannot fall below zero; its upper guard ensures the new value is at most 3. Take subtracts a non-negative amount, so stock cannot rise above 3; amount<=stock ensures it stays at least zero. Those are all permitted actions, so the bounds are preserved. Without the receive upper bound, receiving 4 from stock=0 gives stock=4, a counterexample. The proof assumes integer inputs and these exact guards.
